ENDOCRINE__Pituitary Gland (anterior/pos:
Overview — The “Master Gland”

The pituitary (hypophysis) sits in the sella turcica and links the brain to the endocrine system. It is really two glands of different origin fused together:

🔬 Image slot — pituitary overview — anterior (adenohypophysis) vs posterior (neurohypophysis) with the hypothalamus
Anterior (adenohypophysis)
  • Epithelial/glandular; from Rathke’s pouch (oral ectoderm)
  • Makes & secretes 6 trophic hormones under hypothalamic portal control
Posterior (neurohypophysis)
  • Neural; a downgrowth of the diencephalon (neuroectoderm)
  • Stores & releases ADH & oxytocin made in the hypothalamus
Key split: the anterior lobe synthesises its hormones (glandular); the posterior lobe only stores & releases hormones made by hypothalamic neurons (neural).
How to Recognise Each Lobe on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — anterior pituitary (cords of coloured cells + sinusoids) vs posterior (pale nervous-tissue look)
Anterior
  • Cords & clumps of epithelial cells around sinusoids
  • A mix of colours: pink (acidophils), blue/purple (basophils), pale (chromophobes)
Posterior
  • Pale, looks like nervous tissue — unmyelinated axons + glia (pituicytes)
  • Pink dilatations = Herring bodies (stored neurosecretion)
Colour is the clue: a colourful mix of cell types → anterior; a bland pale “nerve-like” field with Herring bodies → posterior.
Anterior Pituitary Cell Types
StainingCellHormone
Acidophils (pink)SomatotrophGH (growth hormone)
Lactotroph (mammotroph)Prolactin
Basophils (blue/purple)CorticotrophACTH (from POMC)
ThyrotrophTSH
GonadotrophFSH & LH
Chromophobes (pale)Degranulated / stem / null cellsLittle/no granule staining
Mnemonic — basophils = “B-FLAT”: Basophils make FSH, LH, ACTH, TSH. The acidophils make GH & prolactin (“GPA” acids). Definitive typing needs hormone immunohistochemistry.
Hypothalamo-Hypophyseal Portal System (Anterior)
🔬 Image slot — hypophyseal portal system — hypothalamic hormones via median-eminence capillaries to the anterior pituitary
  • Hypothalamic neurons release releasing/inhibiting hormones into a first capillary plexus in the median eminence.
  • Portal veins carry them down the stalk to a second capillary bed that bathes the anterior pituitary cells — a rapid, private delivery route.
Hypothalamic hormoneEffect on anterior pituitary
GHRH / somatostatin↑ / ↓ GH
TRH↑ TSH (& prolactin)
CRH↑ ACTH
GnRH↑ FSH & LH
Dopamine↓ Prolactin (tonic inhibition)
Prolactin is unique: it is under tonic inhibition by dopamine, so stalk damage (loss of dopamine) raises prolactin while lowering the other hormones.
Posterior Pituitary (Neurohypophysis)
🔬 Image slot — posterior pituitary — axons from hypothalamic nuclei, pituicytes and Herring bodies
  • ADH (vasopressin) — made in the supraoptic nucleus; oxytocin — made in the paraventricular nucleus (with overlap).
  • Made in hypothalamic cell bodies, transported down axons of the hypothalamo-hypophyseal tract, and stored in Herring bodies until released into capillaries.
  • Pituicytes are the supporting glial cells; there is no hormone synthesis here.
ADH → collecting-duct water reabsorption + vasoconstriction; oxytocin → uterine contraction & milk let-down. Failure of ADH → diabetes insipidus; excess → SIADH.
Stains
  • H&E — separates acidophils (pink), basophils (blue/purple) & chromophobes (pale) in the anterior lobe.
  • Hormone immunohistochemistry — the definitive way to classify anterior cells & adenomas (e.g. prolactin, GH, ACTH).
  • PAS — basophil (glycoprotein-hormone) granules; useful for corticotrophs.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Prolactinoma
Commonest pituitary adenoma → galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea, low libido; treated with dopamine agonists
GH adenoma
Acromegaly (adults) / gigantism (children)
ACTH adenoma
Cushing disease (pituitary-driven hypercortisolism)
Non-functioning adenoma
Mass effect: bitemporal hemianopia (optic chiasm), hypopituitarism, headache
Sheehan syndrome
Postpartum pituitary infarction (the enlarged gland outgrows its supply) → hypopituitarism (failure to lactate)
Craniopharyngioma
Rathke’s pouch remnant; calcified suprasellar tumour in children (“motor-oil” cyst)
Diabetes insipidus / SIADH
Posterior-lobe/ADH disorders: too little ADH (DI, dilute urine) or too much (SIADH, dilutional hyponatraemia)
Pituitary apoplexy
Sudden haemorrhage/infarction of an adenoma → acute headache, visual loss, hypopituitarism
⭐ Exam Pearls
Anterior = glandular (Rathke’s pouch, makes 6 hormones); posterior = neural (stores ADH & oxytocin).
Acidophils = GH & prolactin; basophils = FSH, LH, ACTH, TSH (“B-FLAT”).
Anterior pituitary is controlled by the hypophyseal portal system (two capillary beds in series).
Prolactin is tonically inhibited by dopamine → stalk section raises prolactin.
Posterior lobe: ADH (supraoptic), oxytocin (paraventricular); stored in Herring bodies; glia = pituicytes.
Prolactinoma = commonest adenoma (dopamine agonist Rx); non-functioning adenoma → bitemporal hemianopia.
Sheehan = postpartum pituitary infarction; craniopharyngioma = Rathke remnant (calcified, children).
ADH problems: too little → diabetes insipidus; too much → SIADH.
ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Gland:
Overview — A Gland That Stores Its Hormone Outside the Cell

The thyroid is unique: it stores hormone extracellularly as colloid inside follicles. It has two cell populations making two very different products.

🔬 Image slot — thyroid at low power — spherical follicles filled with pink colloid, lined by cuboidal cells
Follicular cells
  • Line the follicles; make T3/T4 (thyroid hormone → metabolism)
  • Endodermal origin (from the foramen caecum, descends via the thyroglossal duct)
C (parafollicular) cells
  • Secrete calcitonin (lowers Ca²⁺)
  • Neural-crest origin
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — thyroid follicles — cuboidal follicular epithelium, colloid, and pale parafollicular C cells
  • Spherical follicles filled with homogeneous pink colloid — the diagnostic feature.
  • Follicle wall = simple cuboidal epithelium (follicular cells) whose height reflects activity.
  • C cells — larger, pale cells singly or in small clusters, sitting on the follicular basement membrane (need immunostain to see clearly).
Active gland
  • Tall columnar follicular cells
  • Scant, scalloped colloid (resorption vacuoles)
Inactive gland
  • Flat/squamous follicular cells
  • Abundant, dense colloid
Read the cells for activity: tall cells + scalloped colloid = hyperactive (e.g. Graves); flat cells + packed colloid = inactive/colloid goitre.
Follicular Cells & Thyroid Hormone Synthesis
🔬 Image slot — thyroid hormone synthesis — iodide trapping, thyroglobulin, TPO organification, colloid resorption
1
Iodide trappingNIS pumps iodide into the follicular cell
2
Thyroglobulin + organificationThyroid peroxidase (TPO) iodinates tyrosines on thyroglobulin in the colloid
3
CouplingMIT + DIT → T3; DIT + DIT → T4 (also TPO)
4
Resorption & releaseCells endocytose colloid → lysosomes free T3/T4 into blood
T4 is the main secreted form (a prohormone); it is deiodinated to the more active T3 in the periphery. TPO is the target of antithyroid drugs (carbimazole/PTU) and of anti-TPO antibodies (Hashimoto).
C (Parafollicular) Cells
  • Neural-crest derived; lie within the follicular basement membrane but do not touch the colloid.
  • Secrete calcitonin → lowers serum Ca²⁺ by inhibiting osteoclasts (a minor role in humans, opposite of PTH).
  • Pale cytoplasm with neuroendocrine granules; stain for calcitonin & chromogranin.
C cells are the origin of medullary thyroid carcinoma (calcitonin-secreting, amyloid stroma, linked to MEN 2 / RET).
Regulation
  • TRH (hypothalamus) → TSH (pituitary) → drives follicular-cell growth & hormone synthesis/release.
  • T3/T4 negative feedback onto the pituitary & hypothalamus.
  • Chronic TSH drive (e.g. iodine deficiency) → hyperplasia & goitre.
Iodine paradoxes: a large iodide load transiently inhibits synthesis (Wolff–Chaikoff); in a nodular gland it can instead trigger hyperthyroidism (Jod–Basedow).
Stains & Markers
  • H&E — follicles & colloid; cell height for activity.
  • PAS — colloid (glycoprotein thyroglobulin) is PAS-positive.
  • IHC: thyroglobulin & TTF-1 (follicular cells/differentiated thyroid cancer); calcitonin, chromogranin, CEA (C cells / medullary carcinoma).
  • Congo red — amyloid in medullary carcinoma (apple-green birefringence).
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Graves disease
TSH-receptor antibody → diffuse hyperplasia, tall cells & scalloped colloid; hyperthyroid + eye signs
Hashimoto thyroiditis
Lymphocytic infiltrate + germinal centres & Hurthle cells; anti-TPO; hypothyroid
Multinodular / colloid goitre
Iodine deficiency/TSH drive → enlarged colloid-rich gland with nodules
Papillary carcinoma
Commonest; nuclear features — “Orphan-Annie” clearing, grooves, pseudoinclusions, psammoma bodies; spreads via lymphatics
Follicular carcinoma
Diagnosed by capsular/vascular invasion (not by cytology); haematogenous spread
Medullary carcinoma
C-cell tumour; calcitonin + amyloid stroma; sporadic or MEN 2 (RET)
Thyroglossal duct cyst is a midline neck swelling that moves up with tongue protrusion/swallowing — a remnant of the thyroid’s descent from the foramen caecum.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Thyroid = follicles of colloid lined by cuboidal cells; the only gland that stores hormone extracellularly.
Follicular cells make T3/T4 (metabolism); C cells make calcitonin (lowers Ca, neural-crest).
Cell height = activity: tall + scalloped colloid = active (Graves); flat + packed colloid = inactive.
Synthesis: NIS trap → TPO organification/coupling on thyroglobulin → colloid resorption → T3/T4. TPO = antithyroid-drug & Hashimoto-antibody target.
T4 = main secreted prohormone → deiodinated to active T3 peripherally.
Papillary carcinoma = commonest; Orphan-Annie nuclei, grooves, psammoma bodies; lymphatic spread.
Follicular carcinoma = capsular/vascular invasion; medullary = C cells + amyloid + calcitonin + MEN 2/RET.
Thyroglossal cyst moves with swallowing/tongue protrusion (foramen caecum remnant).
ENDOCRINE__Parathyroid Glands:
Overview — The Calcium Guardians

Usually four tiny glands on the posterior thyroid, the parathyroids run minute-to-minute calcium control by secreting parathyroid hormone (PTH) — the dominant regulator of serum Ca²⁺.

🔬 Image slot — parathyroid at low power — cords of chief cells in a background of adipose tissue
  • Origin: superior glands from the 4th pharyngeal pouch; inferior glands from the 3rd pouch (they descend further, so ectopic/mediastinal glands are usually inferior).
  • Two cell types: chief (principal) cells (make PTH) and oxyphil cells.
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — parathyroid — nests/cords of small pale chief cells with scattered eosinophilic oxyphils and fat
  • Cords & nests of small cells set in a background of mature adipose tissue (fat increases with age — up to ~50% in adults).
  • Chief cells dominate: small, uniform, round central nucleus, pale/pink cytoplasm.
  • Oxyphil cells: fewer, larger, intensely eosinophilic (mitochondria-packed), in clusters.
Fat + two cell types = parathyroid. The intraglandular fat is the fastest way to distinguish it from thyroid (follicles) or a lymph node.
Chief Cells & PTH Secretion
  • Small principal cells with a central round nucleus and pale cytoplasm containing PTH secretory granules.
  • They sense serum Ca²⁺ via the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR): low Ca²⁺ → more PTH; high Ca²⁺ → less PTH (an inverse relationship).
Unusual feedback: PTH is driven directly by the ion it regulates (calcium via CaSR), not by a pituitary trophic hormone.
What PTH Does — Raise Ca, Lower Phosphate
🔬 Image slot — PTH actions on bone, kidney and (via vitamin D) gut
TargetAction
Bone↑ osteoclastic resorption (indirectly, via osteoblast RANKL) → releases Ca²⁺ & phosphate
Kidney↑ Ca²⁺ reabsorption (DCT); ↓ phosphate reabsorption (PCT) → phosphaturia; ↑ 1α-hydroxylase
Gut (indirect)Via activated vitamin D (calcitriol) → ↑ intestinal Ca²⁺ & phosphate absorption
Net effect: ↑ serum Ca²⁺, ↓ serum phosphate (renal phosphate wasting dominates over the phosphate released from bone/gut).
Oxyphil Cells & the Calcium Trio
Oxyphil cells
  • Appear from puberty, increase with age
  • Larger, eosinophilic, packed with mitochondria
  • Function uncertain (little PTH)
The Ca-regulating trio
  • PTH → ↑ Ca (dominant, fast)
  • Calcitriol (vit D) → ↑ gut Ca & phosphate
  • Calcitonin → ↓ Ca (minor in humans)
Stains
  • H&E — chief vs oxyphil cells against intraglandular fat.
  • PTH immunohistochemistry — confirms parathyroid tissue (vs thyroid/thymus/lymph node) and localises adenomas.
  • Intra-operative PTH assay & sestamibi scanning localise overactive glands clinically.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Primary hyperparathyroidism
Usually a single adenoma → ↑PTH, ↑Ca, ↓PO₄; “stones, bones, groans, moans”
Secondary hyperparathyroidism
CKD / vitamin-D deficiency → low Ca → hyperplasia of all glands, ↑PTH with low/normal Ca
Tertiary hyperparathyroidism
Autonomous PTH after long-standing secondary (e.g. post-transplant) → high Ca
Hypoparathyroidism
Post-thyroidectomy or DiGeorge → hypocalcaemia, tetany (Chvostek/Trousseau)
Osteitis fibrosa cystica
Severe hyperparathyroid bone disease → brown tumours, cysts, “salt-and-pepper” skull
Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia
CaSR loss-of-function → mild high Ca with low urine Ca (benign, do not operate)
Parathyroid disease features in MEN 1 (parathyroid + pituitary + pancreas) and MEN 2A (parathyroid + medullary thyroid + phaeochromocytoma).
⭐ Exam Pearls
Four glands; superior = 4th pouch, inferior = 3rd pouch (inferior descends further → ectopic).
Recognise by chief cells + oxyphils in a background of fat (fat rises with age).
Chief cells make PTH; secretion is inversely driven by Ca²⁺ via the CaSR.
PTH: ↑ bone resorption (RANKL), ↑ renal Ca reabsorption, ↓ renal phosphate (phosphaturia), ↑ 1α-hydroxylase → net ↑Ca, ↓PO₄.
Oxyphil cells = larger, eosinophilic, mitochondria-rich, appear at puberty, unclear role.
Primary HPT = adenoma (high Ca); secondary = CKD/low vit D hyperplasia; tertiary = autonomous.
FHH (CaSR mutation) = high Ca + low urine Ca — do not operate.
Severe HPT bone disease = osteitis fibrosa cystica / brown tumours; MEN 1 & 2A involve parathyroids.
